content: 1. Comparative studies of laboratory and clinical monitoring in individuals with HIV have shown that those receiving tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) are at an increased risk of reduced estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) but do not exhibit an increased risk of renal failure over a median follow-up period of five years. This evidence is rated as low-certainty. 2. In children and adolescents, TDF has been associated with decreases in bone mineral density (BMD). However, the long-term implications of reduced BMD on growth patterns or fracture risk remain uncertain. 3. A randomized controlled trial (RCT) involving adolescents aged 12–17 years receiving TDF found that none of the participants met the safety endpoint of a 6% decrease in spine BMD at week 72. 4. There is uncertainty regarding the optimal methods to measure and monitor TDF-related bone toxicity in children. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) testing is not widely available and does not detect osteomalacia. Careful growth monitoring is recommended for children undergoing TDF treatment. 5. Recent data from the CHAPAS trial support the safety of tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) in children living with HIV. 6. The safety profile of entecavir (ETV) in children is consistent with that observed in adults, with no reported renal adverse events over 48 weeks in an ongoing ETV trial (AI463289) submitted to the FDA. 7. TAF has been evaluated in clinical trials for hepatitis B during late pregnancy and appears to be safe and effective. However, despite no major safety concerns in cohort studies, TAF has not yet been approved for the prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of hepatitis B. 8. Limited data exist on the optimal assays for monitoring TDF-related renal toxicity. Some individuals may have normal serum creatinine levels but impaired renal function, suggesting that reliance on absolute serum creatinine values may lead to inappropriate TDF administration in those with pre-existing kidney disease. 9. A high frequency of glycosuria has been observed in non-diabetic individuals undergoing biopsy for TDF nephrotoxicity. Increased serum creatinine levels in these individuals, compared to TDF-treated individuals with normal GFR, suggest that dipstick testing for glycosuria may serve as a cost-effective screening tool for serious TDF-induced kidney injury. 10. Switching from TDF to TAF has been shown to maintain or improve suppression of hepatitis B virus (HBV) replication while improving bone and renal safety, particularly in individuals with stage 2 chronic kidney disease. 11. Due to its improved renal safety profile, TAF is preferred over other nucleoside analogues for individuals at risk of bone or renal complications, older adults, and those with evidence of impaired renal function. 12. In 2015, the Guidelines Development Group conditionally recommended annual monitoring of renal function, growth monitoring in children, baseline renal function assessment, and risk categorization for renal dysfunction based on limited evidence. 13. TAF is now recommended in special circumstances for individuals with established osteoporosis and/or impaired kidney function, as well as an alternative regimen for adolescents aged 12 years or older. 14. The indications for TAF could be extended to individuals with an eGFR higher than 60 mL/min. Switching to TAF has been associated with improved kidney function, particularly in those with stage 2 chronic kidney disease, given the long-term use of nucleoside analogues in most individuals. 15. More individuals treated with TAF than TDF achieve normal alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels, although the mechanism for this remains unknown. 16. The 2021 WHO consolidated HIV guidelines do not consider baseline creatinine measurement an absolute requirement for initiating antiretroviral therapy with a preferred TDF-based regimen in people living with HIV. This also applies to initiating antiviral therapy for chronic hepatitis B (CHB). 17. Monitoring for renal dysfunction progression is advised periodically for individuals at low risk of renal toxicity. TAF or ETV is recommended for individuals with impaired baseline eGFR (<50 mL/min) or those at higher risk of renal toxicity, such as older adults, those with underlying renal disease, long-term diabetes, uncontrolled hypertension, or those receiving nephrotoxic drugs. 18. Most cases of tubular dysfunction associated with TDF are reversible, and the risk of renal impairment can be reduced by adjusting the dose based on renal function monitoring. 19. Individuals switching from TDF to TAF require ongoing monitoring of renal function, BMD, lipid profiles, weight, and metabolic syndrome. 20. The renal toxicity of TDF primarily affects the renal tubules, and glomerular function tests do not adequately measure tubular dysfunction. However, there are currently no simple tests to detect renal tubular toxicity. 21. Monitoring may include serum creatinine, estimated GFR (using the MDRD formula), serum phosphate, and urine dipstick tests for proteinuria and glycosuria. Growth monitoring is recommended for children and adolescents using TDF. 22. Resource limitations in some settings may restrict access to creatinine testing. Simple urine dipstick testing is a more affordable alternative in lowand middle-income countries. 23. Known risk factors for TDF-induced nephrotoxicity include underlying renal dysfunction, low CD4 count, low body weight, comorbid hypertension, diabetes, HIV-associated kidney disease, HIV or hepatitis C coinfection, and TDF use with ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitors in people with HIV infection. Managing these comorbid conditions should be prioritized. 24. Individuals receiving TAF should be monitored for weight gain, lipid increases, and metabolic syndrome. Age and advanced liver disease are additional factors that can help identify those at greatest risk of osteoporotic fractures. 25. DEXA can be used to monitor BMD changes in individuals receiving TDF. The frequency of monitoring depends on the individual’s age and health status. 26. TDF-containing regimens may be replaced with non-TDF-containing regimens for individuals at higher risk of fragility fractures. 27. Surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) with abdominal ultrasound and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) testing every six months is recommended for individuals with cirrhosis, a family history of HCC, or those older than 40 years with HBV DNA levels >20,000 IU/mL. 28. Effective surveillance programs are essential for detecting HCC at an early stage, increasing the chances of effective treatment. However, continued surveillance poses a substantial financial burden, even in high-income countries. 29. Current surveillance strategies for HCC include ultrasound and AFP measurement every six months. These strategies detect HCC at an earlier stage and improve survival rates. 30. Research gaps include evaluating the cost-effectiveness of routine renal function monitoring for all individuals receiving long-term TDF or ETV versus targeted monitoring for high-risk individuals, developing simplified monitoring tools, and establishing the long-term safety and efficacy of TAF compared to TDF.
